---
title: Overview
---

This project provides a structured examination of the data science lifecycle, focusing on the core stages of data collection, cleaning, exploratory data analysis (EDA), and modeling through both supervised and unsupervised methods. The emphasis is placed less on final predictive performance or conclusions and more on the underlying processes, assumptions, and methodological decisions that shape each stage.

Data collection is conducted using the Python library `pybaseball`, which serves as a wrapper for multiple baseball data sources, including FanGraphs and Statcast. This approach highlights how modern data science workflows often rely on APIs and abstraction layers to efficiently gather large, heterogeneous datasets from multiple providers.

The data cleaning phase centers on constructing a unified and analysis-ready dataset in the form of a Pandas `DataFrame`, ultimately exported as a CSV file. Each row corresponds to a single MLB hitter's season from 2017 through 2024, while each column represents a relevant performance metric. These features span traditional counting statistics (e.g., home runs), advanced sabermetrics (e.g., weighted runs created), and Statcast-derived measures (e.g., maximum home run distance). Particular attention is given to handling missing values, aligning data across sources, and ensuring consistency in labels and units.

The EDA is meant to identify patterns, relationships, and potential anomalies within the dataset. Visualization tools such as `matplotlib` and `plotly` are employed to generate a variety of plots, including correlation heatmaps, distributions, and pairwise comparisons. This stage emphasizes interpretability and intuition-building, illustrating how different statistical measures relate to one another and how underlying structure in the data can inform subsequent modeling choices.

The modeling component introduces several foundational machine learning techniques within this baseball analytics context. These include univariate linear regression for examining simple relationships, multivariate logistic regression for classification tasks, and clustering algorithms for uncovering latent groupings among players or seasons. Rather than optimizing model performance, the focus is on understanding how these algorithms operate, what assumptions they make, and how they respond to in the baseball statistics domain.
